items.stem: The government of a country with a Westminster-style Parliament wants to introduce a new law on the regulation of artificial intelligence. The minister, Felix, is unsure whether to consult before drafting the Bill and how long the process will take. Describe to Felix the stages through which the Bill must pass before it becomes law. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: a Green Paper may be published for consultation, followed by a White Paper of firm proposals; first reading is formal; second reading is the main debate and vote on principles; committee stage examines each clause and may amend; report stage considers amendments; third reading is a final vote; the Bill then goes through the same stages in the House of Lords; the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 limit the Lords to delay; Royal Assent turns the Bill into an Act. Application: Felix should consult on the regulation of artificial intelligence because the issue is technical and affects many groups; with a government majority the Bill is likely to pass the Commons; if the Lords object they can delay but not normally block the Bill; the Act may also need commencement orders before it takes effect. Conclusion: The Bill on the regulation of artificial intelligence can become law once it has passed all stages in both Houses and received Royal Assent, which may take many months.

items.stem: Define the term 'parliamentary sovereignty'.
items.answer: The principle that Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can make or unmake any law, no Parliament can bind its successors and no court can override or set aside an Act of Parliament.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. the principle that Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can make or unmake any law, no Parliament can bind its successors and no court can override or set aside an Act of Parliament. [2]

items.stem: Kwame claims that a section of the Housing Act 2018, an Act of Parliament, is invalid because MPs were misled about its effect during the debate. Kwame asks the High Court to declare the section void. Advise Kwame whether the court can declare the section void.
items.answer: Law: parliamentary sovereignty: no court can override or set aside an Act of Parliament (Dicey); in Pickin v British Railways Board (1974) the courts refused to question the validity of an Act; Parliament cannot bind its successors and a later Act impliedly repeals an inconsistent earlier one; under the Human Rights Act 1998 the court may only make a declaration of incompatibility. Application: Kwame's argument that MPs were misled about its effect during the debate does not allow the court to strike down the Housing Act 2018; the court must apply the Act as it stands. Conclusion: The court cannot declare the section void; Kwame would have to persuade Parliament to change the law.

items.stem: A national emergency caused by a major earthquake has hit the country. Parliament is not sitting and urgent rules are needed to ration fuel supplies. Diego, a government lawyer, is asked how this can be done. Advise Diego on the most suitable form of law-making and any safeguards. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: Orders in Council are made by the King and Privy Council; the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 allows emergency regulations when there is not time to pass an Act; emergency regulations must be laid before Parliament and lapse after 30 days unless approved. Application: the emergency caused by a major earthquake creates an urgent need that the slow Bill procedure cannot meet; safeguards ensure Parliament can still scrutinise the regulations. Conclusion: An Order in Council under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004 is the appropriate method, subject to later parliamentary approval.

items.stem: The Fisheries Management Act (fictional) 2017 requires the minister to consult "organisations representing small fishing businesses" before making regulations. Minister Tomás made regulations about safety inspections without consulting the Small Operators Association, which represents small fishing businesses. Advise the Small Operators Association whether the regulations can be challenged. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: delegated legislation must follow the procedure in the enabling Act; failure to consult as required is procedural ultra vires (Aylesbury Mushrooms 1972); consultation must be genuine and allow adequate time (ex p NUT 2000); the challenge is by judicial review in the Administrative Court. Application: the Fisheries Management Act (fictional) 2017 required consultation with bodies representing small fishing businesses; the Small Operators Association was not consulted, so the procedure was not followed; as in Aylesbury Mushrooms the regulations may be invalid at least against the Small Operators Association. Conclusion: The regulations are likely to be held procedurally ultra vires and invalid in relation to the Small Operators Association.

items.stem: A Bill on banning trail hunting with dogs has been passed by the House of Commons, but the House of Lords voted it down six months ago. The Bill is not a money Bill. Mei, a government minister, asks whether it can still become law. Advise Mei whether the Bill can become law without the agreement of the House of Lords. In your answer, refer to decided cases and assess how a court is likely to decide.
items.answer: Law: under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords can delay a non-money Bill for about one year; the Bill must be passed by the Commons in two successive sessions, then it can receive Royal Assent without the Lords' consent; R (Jackson) v Attorney-General (2005) confirmed that Acts passed in this way are valid; by the Salisbury convention the Lords do not usually oppose manifesto Bills at second reading. Application: the Bill on banning trail hunting with dogs is not a money Bill, so the one-year delay applies; the Commons should pass it again in the next session; after that it can be presented for Royal Assent without the Lords. Conclusion: The Bill can become law without the Lords' consent by using the Parliament Acts procedure, after a delay of about one year.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'parliamentary sovereignty'.
items.answer: The principle that Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can make or unmake any law, no Parliament can bind its successors and no court can override or set aside an Act of Parliament.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. the principle that Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can make or unmake any law, no Parliament can bind its successors and no court can override or set aside an Act of Parliament. [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the rule that Parliament cannot bind its successors.
items.answer: Each Parliament is sovereign, so a later Parliament can repeal or amend any Act passed by an earlier one; an Act cannot be entrenched against future change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: later Parliament can repeal/amend any earlier Act; 1 mark: no Act can be entrenched, e.g. implied repeal (Ellen Street Estates). [2]

items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, "The House of Lords plays a valuable role in the law-making process." Discuss.
items.answer: For: the Lords revises and improves Bills, using expertise of members; it can ask the Commons to think again on controversial measures; it is less dominated by party politics, with many crossbench members. Against: its members are unelected, so it lacks democratic legitimacy; its powers are limited by the Parliament Acts, so it can only delay; the Salisbury convention means it rarely opposes manifesto commitments. Conclusion: The Lords is a valuable revising chamber but its lack of democratic legitimacy rightly limits its powers.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of the controls over delegated legislation. Support your answer with relevant authority.
items.answer: For: the affirmative resolution procedure gives real scrutiny for important SIs; judicial review can strike down ultra vires legislation (Aylesbury Mushrooms, Fire Brigades Union); consultation with experts improves quality. Against: most SIs use the negative procedure and are never debated; the Joint Committee cannot amend SIs and its reports are often ignored; judicial review depends on a challenge being brought, is costly and only covers legality; wide enabling Acts leave little room for ultra vires. Conclusion: The controls exist but are of limited effectiveness given the volume of delegated legislation.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge and understanding [4]: accurate explanation of the law with supporting authority, e.g. Aylesbury Mushrooms (1972); ex p Fire Brigades Union (1995); Strickland v Hayes BC (1896); Wednesbury (1948); R (Public Law Project) v Lord Chancellor (2016). AO3 Analysis and evaluation [6]: arguments supporting the view, e.g. the affirmative resolution procedure gives real scrutiny for important SIs; judicial review can strike down ultra vires legislation (Aylesbury Mushrooms, Fire Brigades Union); consultation with experts improves quality; arguments against / problems, e.g. most SIs use the negative procedure and are never debated; the Joint Committee cannot amend SIs and its reports are often ignored; judicial review depends on a challenge being brought, is costly and only covers legality; wide enabling Acts leave little room for ultra vires. Levels: L1 basic, descriptive points; L2 some accurate law with limited comment; L3 accurate law and some developed evaluation; L4 wide-ranging, accurate law with sustained, balanced evaluation and a reasoned conclusion.
